title: Python asyncio Tasks: Structured Concurrency, Cancellation & Timeouts
summary: Dense study notes on running concurrent work safely with asyncio tasks. Covers create_task and task references, gather vs TaskGroup and exception groups, cancellation and CancelledError, shield, timeouts, and structured concurrency patterns in Python 3.11+.

chapters.title: Coroutines, Tasks and the Event Loop
points: A coroutine function (async def) returns a coroutine object when called, and none of its body runs until the object is awaited or scheduled
Awaiting a coroutine directly runs it inline and sequentially: `await a(); await b()` gives no concurrency
A Task wraps a coroutine and schedules it on the event loop so it runs concurrently with the caller
Task is a subclass of Future: it has .done(), .result(), .exception(), .cancel(), .cancelled() and add_done_callback()
The event loop is single-threaded and cooperative: tasks switch only at an await that actually suspends
A blocking call such as time.sleep() or CPU-bound code freezes every task, so use await asyncio.sleep() or asyncio.to_thread() instead
asyncio.run(main()) creates the loop, runs main to completion, cancels the tasks still pending, then closes the loop
asyncio.current_task() returns the running Task, and asyncio.all_tasks() returns the set of tasks that are not done
Example: two `await asyncio.sleep(1)` calls take 2s sequentially but 1s as two tasks
Mistake: calling a coroutine function without awaiting it makes Python warn 'coroutine ... was never awaited', and the work never runs

chapters.title: create_task and Keeping References
points: asyncio.create_task(coro, *, name=None, context=None) schedules coro on the running loop and returns a Task at once
The task starts at the next await point of the caller, not inside the create_task call
The event loop keeps only weak references to tasks, so a task with no strong reference can be garbage-collected mid-run
Fire-and-forget bug: `asyncio.create_task(send_email())` with the result discarded can vanish silently
Fix pattern: `background = set(); t = create_task(c); background.add(t); t.add_done_callback(background.discard)`
An exception in a task that is never awaited is only logged as 'Task exception was never retrieved' when the task is garbage-collected
Use name= or task.set_name() so tasks are identifiable in debug output and in asyncio.all_tasks() dumps
context= (3.11+) runs the task in a specific contextvars.Context; by default it gets a copy of the current context
Python 3.12 added asyncio.eager_task_factory: the task runs synchronously until its first suspension, which saves a loop iteration
Prefer TaskGroup.create_task over bare create_task: the group holds the reference and awaits the task for you

chapters.title: asyncio.gather
points: `await asyncio.gather(*aws, return_exceptions=False)` runs awaitables concurrently and returns their results as a list
Results come back in argument order, not in completion order
Bare coroutines passed to gather are wrapped in Tasks automatically
With return_exceptions=False, the first exception propagates to the awaiter, but the other tasks are not cancelled and keep running
With return_exceptions=True, exceptions are returned in the result list in place of values, and nothing is raised
If gather itself is cancelled, every child that has not finished is cancelled too
If one child is cancelled, it is treated as raising CancelledError, and the gather is not cancelled
The tasks left running after a failure become orphans: nobody awaits them, and their errors are lost
Example: `r1, r2 = await gather(fetch(a), fetch(b))` unpacks the results in order
Still fine for simple fan-out when you want partial results via return_exceptions=True

chapters.title: TaskGroup (Python 3.11+)
points: `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: t = tg.create_task(coro())` starts child tasks bound to the block
Leaving the async with block waits for every child task to finish, so no task outlives the block
When the first child raises a non-CancelledError exception, the group cancels all the remaining children and the body
All child failures are collected and raised together as an ExceptionGroup (a BaseExceptionGroup if a BaseException is involved)
KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit raised in a child are re-raised directly, not wrapped
Read results after the block with t.result(); each task object is the handle
An exception raised in the async with body also cancels the children
Calling tg.create_task on a group that has already finished raises RuntimeError
Comparison: gather leaves siblings running on failure, while TaskGroup cancels them and reports every error
Comparison: gather returns an ordered list, while TaskGroup gives you the Task handles and collects results explicitly

chapters.title: Exception Groups and except*
points: ExceptionGroup(msg, [excs]) (PEP 654, 3.11) carries several unrelated exceptions at once, and .exceptions holds the tuple
BaseExceptionGroup is the base; ExceptionGroup can only contain Exception subclasses
`except* ValueError as eg:` matches the ValueError leaves, and eg is an ExceptionGroup of just those
Several except* clauses can run for one group, one per matching type, unlike plain except
Unmatched leaves are re-raised automatically as a smaller group after the except* clauses run
You cannot mix except and except* in the same try statement, and except* cannot use break, continue or return
Plain `except ValueError` does not catch an ExceptionGroup that contains a ValueError, which is a common TaskGroup trap
eg.subgroup(pred) keeps the matching leaves, and eg.split(pred) returns a (match, rest) pair
Groups can nest; traceback printing shows a tree of every sub-exception
Example: `try: async with TaskGroup()... except* TimeoutError: retry() except* ValueError: log()`

chapters.title: Cancellation and CancelledError
points: task.cancel(msg=None) requests cancellation: CancelledError is thrown into the coroutine at its next await
cancel() returns False if the task is already done; otherwise it returns True, and the request is not yet completed
CancelledError subclasses BaseException (since 3.8), so a bare `except Exception` does not swallow it
Do cleanup in try/finally or in `except CancelledError: cleanup(); raise`, always re-raising
Swallowing CancelledError makes the task ignore the cancellation, which breaks TaskGroup, timeout() and shutdown
task.cancelled() is True only if the task ended by raising CancelledError
Awaiting a cancelled task raises CancelledError in the awaiter
task.cancelling() (3.11) counts the pending cancel requests, and task.uncancel() decrements the count
TaskGroup and asyncio.timeout use cancelling() and uncancel() to tell their own cancellations from outside ones
Example: `t.cancel(); try: await t except CancelledError: pass` is the standard way to stop a background task

chapters.title: asyncio.shield
points: `await asyncio.shield(aw)` protects the inner awaitable from being cancelled when the outer task is cancelled
If the outer task is cancelled, the outer await still raises CancelledError, but the inner task keeps running
shield wraps a coroutine in a Task, so keep a strong reference to the inner task or it may be garbage-collected
shield does not protect against cancelling the inner task directly (inner.cancel())
Use case: finishing a DB commit or payment write that must not be torn half-way through
Pattern: `t = create_task(commit()); try: await shield(t) except CancelledError: await t; raise`
Comparison: shield hides the cancellation from the inner work, while try/finally runs cleanup after the cancellation
Mistake: shielding everything turns tasks into uncancellable zombies that block shutdown and TaskGroup exit
At shutdown, asyncio.run still cancels leftover shielded tasks, so shield is not durability

chapters.title: Timeouts: asyncio.timeout vs wait_for
points: `async with asyncio.timeout(5):` (3.11+) bounds everything inside the block, and None means no deadline
Mechanism: at the deadline it cancels the current task, then turns CancelledError into TimeoutError when the block exits
Catch TimeoutError outside the async with block; inside the block you only ever see CancelledError
asyncio.TimeoutError is an alias of the builtin TimeoutError since 3.11
asyncio.timeout_at(when) takes an absolute loop.time() deadline, and cm.reschedule(new_when) moves the deadline
`await asyncio.wait_for(aw, timeout)` wraps one awaitable, cancels it on timeout, waits for the cancellation to finish, then raises TimeoutError
Since 3.12, wait_for is implemented on top of asyncio.timeout
`asyncio.wait(tasks, timeout=, return_when=FIRST_COMPLETED)` never cancels anything and returns a (done, pending) pair
Comparison: timeout() covers a block of several awaits, wait_for covers one awaitable, and wait covers many without cancelling
Mistake: a task that swallows CancelledError makes the timeout hang or never fire
Nested timeouts: the innermost expiry raises; an outer expiry is distinguished via the task's cancelling() count

chapters.title: Structured Concurrency in Practice
points: Structured concurrency: every task's lifetime is bounded by a lexical scope, and the scope does not exit until its children finish
Guarantees: no orphaned tasks, errors always propagate to the parent, and cancelling a parent cancels its subtree
Origin: Trio nurseries (Nathaniel J. Smith's 'go statement considered harmful'); TaskGroup is asyncio's nursery
Pass the tg into helpers (`def spawn_workers(tg): tg.create_task(...)`) instead of spawning free-floating tasks
Long-lived background services belong in a TaskGroup opened in main() so they shut down with the app
Limit fan-out by combining asyncio.Semaphore(n) with TaskGroup: `async with sem: await fetch(u)`
Producer/consumer: an asyncio.Queue plus a TaskGroup of workers, with queue.join() and a sentinel for shutdown
Blocking or CPU work goes through `await asyncio.to_thread(fn)` so the loop stays responsive
Trade-off: gather with return_exceptions=True gives partial results, while TaskGroup gives fail-fast and clean cancellation
Checklist: no bare create_task, re-raise CancelledError, shield sparingly, catch errors with except*

chapters.title: asyncio Tasks Cheatsheet
points: Spawn: `async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg: t = tg.create_task(c())`, then read t.result() after the block
Fire-and-forget: keep the task in a set and add `add_done_callback(set.discard)`
gather: ordered results; siblings are not cancelled on error; return_exceptions=True gives partial results
TaskGroup: fail-fast, cancels siblings, raises an ExceptionGroup
Handle groups: `except* ValueError as eg:` and eg.exceptions; plain except misses a group
Cancel: `t.cancel()`, then `await t` inside `except CancelledError`
CancelledError is a BaseException, so clean up and re-raise
Protect a critical write: keep a reference to the inner task, then `await asyncio.shield(t)`
Deadline for a block: `async with asyncio.timeout(s)`, catching TimeoutError outside
Deadline for one awaitable: `await asyncio.wait_for(aw, s)`; wait without cancelling: `asyncio.wait(..., timeout=s)`
Blocking or CPU work: `await asyncio.to_thread(fn)`; bounded fan-out: Semaphore
Version map: 3.8 CancelledError becomes a BaseException; 3.11 adds TaskGroup, timeout and except*; 3.12 adds eager_task_factory and moves wait_for onto timeout
